body_markdown:
> Cars are not jewelry.
> They can get wet.
> They can get dirty.


Tom Cotter’s motto for the annual rally he and Jim Maxwell organize for the Shelby Cobra would make a great bumper sticker. For the past 20 years, the duo has invited adventurous Cobra owners—meaning people who own the genuine article, not one of the many available Cobra reproductions—to add miles to the odometers of their cars. Cars that are[valued at about a million dollars](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/shelby/cobra/1966/1966-shelby-cobra-427_(csx3101_~_csx3200)?id=aCn1I000000DLoVSAW) . Their most recent sortie occurred at one of my favorite driving destinations—the Hocking Hills in southern Ohio—so for a couple of days last May, I hitched a ride with the Shelby caravan.


The Cotter-Maxwell rally was inspired by a chance encounter between Cotter and Carroll Shelby himself—more on that in a bit. As you might know, Cotter hosts the[Barn Find Hunter video series](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=L7p8-TccjTk&list=PLHKCmmH-x9mLN0PNeFBtxyZ7olwptkO5q) on Hagerty’s[YouTube channel](https://www.youtube.com/@Hagerty) , taking us into countless barns, sheds, garages, and other hiding places to reveal automotive treasures. Cotter’s natural charisma and energy, plus plenty of pluck and smarts, helped him build a successful automotive PR business in North Carolina, which he sold in 2001, enabling him to buy his dream car, a Shelby Cobra.


The seed for Cotter’s Cobra dream was planted early on, when he was in grade school. Someone gave him a cover for a school textbook featuring a drawing of a Cobra. Not only was the cover more attractive than the brown paper grocery bags we all used, but it also cemented Shelby’s sports car in Cotter’s young brain. Maxwell, for his part, is an enthusiast from Greensboro, North Carolina, who’s nurtured a lifelong Cobra lust, as well. He bought his first one in 1987 and added a 427 in 2000. When Cotter started shopping for his own Cobra, Maxwell helped him identify a good car. “I had heard horror stories about fake Cobras presented as real ones,” Cotter says. “So I reached out to Jim to learn all I could before committing to a car.” Maxwell rolled out the vehicular red carpet, and the two spent an afternoon driving his cars. A lifelong friendship blossomed.


Cotter ended up buying a largely original 1965 Shelby 289 Cobra in Walnut Creek, California, for $167,500. “Everyone told me I paid too much.” He didn’t care. He’d just realized his automotive fantasy, and what better way to celebrate than to drive it home? Cotter invited *Road & Track* writer Peter Egan to come along. Egan chronicled the nine-day journey, which added another 3300 miles to the 40,000 already on the odometer, in the pages of the magazine.


A few years later, while at a Shelby American Automobile Club (SAAC) event, Cotter was under his car looking for the source of a clunking noise. “What are you doing under there?” someone gruffly asked. Imagine Cotter’s surprise when he got out from under the car and learned that the voice belonged to none other than Carroll Shelby. “Is this the car that went cross country?” Shelby inquired. Cotter confirmed that indeed it was.


“Now that’s what I’m talking about,” Shelby continued. “I didn’t build no trailer queens.” The starstruck Cotter felt like he’d been kissed by the Pope. Inspired by Shelby’s blessing, Cotter suggested to Maxwell that they should organize a Cobra tour with other owners who weren’t afraid to take Shelby’s advice. There were two common bonds to tie everyone together: passion for the Cobra and, critically, actually using them—getting them wet, getting them dirty.


The formula worked. In 2006, about a half-dozen cars and 12 people—significant others are encouraged to attend—joined Cotter and Maxwell in the Smoky Mountains for several days of raucous driving. The roster has grown to as many as 30 cars, Shelby Mustangs are now invited as well, and the rally has been held across the U.S. and[even Alaska](https://www.hagerty.com/media/archived/289-shelby-cobra-bear-tom-cotter/) . Most of the owners I met in Ohio had been to a majority of the rallies. True altruists, Cotter and Maxwell only charge for expenses.


Cameron Neveu


## Cobra the Car, Cobra the Story


Although it’s the cars that brought these Cobra owners to the Hocking Hills, the stories behind the cars are the glue that binds them. Hanging out with this passionate group, I heard all the lore that makes the Cobra and the period in which Shelby created it so compelling.


Born in 1923 in Leesburg, Texas, Carroll Shelby had a knack for racing and for business. He won the 24 Hours of Le Mans with Aston Martin in 1959, but a heart condition forced him to retire from racing. He pivoted to car building, deciding to pair a powerful American V-8 with a lightweight European chassis. With a supply of Ford’s new 260-cubic-inch V-8 engines, Shelby approached AC Cars in England for its lightweight aluminum-bodied car called the Ace. In early 1962, an Ace fitted with the Ford powertrain emerged from Dean Moon’s Southern California shop. The Shelby Cobra, serial number CSX2000, was born, and Carroll Shelby made sports car history.


Shelby produced some 75 Cobras that year. In 1963, the Cobra was upgraded with a 289-cubic-inch version of the V-8. Shelby added a new model in 1965 with[Ford’s larger 427-cubic-inch](https://www.hagerty.com/media/automotive-history/an-ode-to-fords-427/) big-block V-8. In the five years of Shelby Cobra production, Shelby built 655 Cobras with the small-block V-8 and 343 with the big motor, just under 1000 total cars.


Dennis Greene (not pictured) owns this Cobra along with a number of others. He bought his first at age 18 for $1000.


Cameron Neveu


That’s the CliffsNotes version. Shelby’s decade from roughly 1960 to 1970 would make anyone wonder if the man ever slept. Along with the Cobra, he developed and manufactured[high-performance Mustangs](https://www.hagerty.com/media/magazine-features/25-greatest-mustangs-shelby-gt350-h/) , and Ford also hired him to develop and[race the GT40](https://www.hagerty.com/media/magazine-features/hagerty-magazine/real-story-behind-ford-v-ferrari/) to compete with Ferrari at Le Mans. In 1966, the GT40 took the top three places at the French endurance race. Additionally, Shelby American extensively raced the Cobra, and the[Shelby Daytona coupe](https://www.hagerty.com/media/market-trends/sotw-monterey-edition/) won its class at Le Mans in 1964, beating the Ferrari GTO.


Hundreds of books have been written about Shelby, and rightly so. He assembled an enormously talented group of fabricators and racers, mostly SoCal hot rodders, whose collective automotive and racing achievements defy belief.


## The 289 Cobra


Ohio’s rural two-lanes are some of the best in the country. They’re even better with a bunch of Cobras on them.


Cameron Neveu


The doors of Roger Morrison’s light blue 289 provide perfect elbow perches as we glide along Ohio’s stunning State Route 78. At the moderate speeds Morrison is driving, the airflow massages the scalp rather than pummeling the face. “Cobras are as fun at 25 mph as they are at 125,” says Morrison.


Like most members of the group, he’s had his car for decades. Mike McCluskey, one of a handful of celebrated Cobra whisperers, restored it and added touring-friendly features like a tall rear end and wide-ratio gearbox. “Why not take advantage of the low-end torque?” Morrison asks.


Once he surrenders the wheel to me, I see what he means: The Cobra scoots no matter where the rev counter sits. It wants to hustle. The large steering wheel is presumably there to alleviate the high efforts that a front-mounted engine and manual steering might have required, but Popeye forearms are not required. The steering is light and communicative once underway, and the shifter is as easy to use as a Miata’s.


The pure performance reminds me why driving coaches of the era worshipped at the altar of smoothness. The car gracefully arcs into corners and then squats, under power, at the exit. On Ohio’s byways, I could do this all day. Or all month.


> Two common bonds tied everyone together: passion for the Cobra and actually using them.


Although the Cobra is basically a British chassis and a Ford engine mashed together, Morrison’s Cobra does not feel like a Frankenstein. The brakes, shifter, and steering are integrated in such a way that they fade from my consciousness. I’m just driving, thinking about the correct speed and trajectory, but not the tools that get there. I’m in a flow state.


There is no dedicated mechanic or chase vehicle on the tour. Rather, everyone brings along a few tools in their trunk and helps one another with adjustments and repairs as needed.


Cameron Neveu


That morning, I’d heard stories over breakfast that Shelby thought his band of fabricators and assemblers didn’t really figure out the Cobra until they’d built 300 of them. By then, the original English Smiths gauges had been replaced with ones from the Ford parts bin, a rack-and-pinion steering rack was sourced from the MGB, and all sorts of other small modifications had been made. Morrison’s car, chassis number CSX2181, is emblematic of the Cobra’s evolution. It has the Smiths gauges, but also the MGB rack.


A cow springs out of the roadside scrub, right in our path. I miss it and glance at Morrison, expecting a panicked expression. “Well,” he says, coolly. “If you’d hit it, that would have matched the deer I hit with the other side last year.” The repairs for that, including a full respray, were covered by his Hagerty policy.


Morrison’s wife of 60 years, who had been a regular in the Cobra group, passed away a couple of weeks before the Ohio tour. The loss, while not unexpected after an illness, was felt by all. For Morrison, the uplifting support of the group was helping him cope. “That says a lot about our hobby.”


Greene (right) helps fellow Cobra owner Paul Gould with carburetor issues.


Cameron Neveu


## Worn In, Not Out


“You hear that?” Cotter asks. He’s pointing out an exhaust resonance that only occurs at 3500 rpm in fourth gear. “I just love that.” Moments later, his car clicks past 90,000 miles.


Cotter has never stopped tinkering with his car, installing Flowmaster mufflers and a vintage suitcase, festooned with stickers, for the rear luggage rack. He stashes moving blankets in the trunk to protect the lithe aluminum bodywork from hail. He has stuffed foam pool noodles into body cavities to insulate from the heat, but they have a marginal effect—the cramped footbox on these cars sometimes heats the pedals enough to burnish shoe soles.


During the 50,000 miles he has put on the car, the aluminum body has started to tear, a known Cobra problem caused by the flexible chassis. The fix is to stiffen the chassis by sleeving the two longitudinal chassis rails that run the length of the car. That modification didn’t overly stiffen his car, which conforms to the road yet tracks straight and still handles sharply. It’s the kind of just-right ride and handling balance I’ve long admired in Lotus sports cars—SoCal hot rodders knew how to achieve it, too.


Original Cobra toolsets are rare and worth thousands of dollars.


Cameron Neveu


Despite its mileage and age, Cotter’s Cobra feels tightly screwed together. Perhaps that’s because he maintains it so diligently. “They’re relatively simple cars,” he says, “and an advantage over other classic roadsters is that I can probably fix any problem as long as I can find a parts store.”


Another advantage is horsepower and torque. Cotter’s Cobra effortlessly keeps up with modern traffic and can make quick use of even short passing zones. What it’s not, however, is so unruly that the driver is scared to lean on it. That’s one of the reasons Cotter sought out a 289 car and not a 427. “I can see how everyone gets excited about the 427 and the bulging fenders and all, but the one you want is the 289,” he says.


Maxwell is co-organizer of the tour.


Cameron Neveu


## OK. But What About That 427?


There was only one 427 Cobra at this rally, owned by Dennis Greene. When he had a family matter to attend to, he threw me the keys. Right place, right time.


Ford built the 427 engine for NASCAR as part of Henry Ford II’s Total Performance racing campaign. It came out in 1962, and by 1964, the Shelby crew had extensively modified the Ace chassis to accommodate the physically larger engine, using larger-diameter frame rails and spreading them farther apart. The body sprouted beefy fender bulges and a prominent hood scoop. Coil springs, rather than leaf springs, were fitted to the rear axle. From the cockpit, the car feels bigger. Its gearshifter, positioned farther rearward, meets the driver’s hand with a long rod that finds the gears by moving up and down, not fore and aft.


There is nothing subtle about the 427. The throttle is a chaos maker, eager to light up the rear tires in any gear. “If you mash the gas,” Greene warns, “be ready to gather it up.” It feels brutish and unruly, like a barrel-chested pit bull pulling at the end of a leash. Its hint of danger, however, is part of the rush. The 427 beckons you, dares you: Come on, big man, let’s see what you’ve got.


Nick Acton, who owns a Cobra restoration and repair business in New Hampshire, rides shotgun with the author.


Cameron Neveu


The hyper-caffeinated throttle response rockets the car between corners. I’m kind of scared but thrilled, too. The engine and modifications added 300 pounds to the 2200-pound 289, yet that engine makes the 427 feel weightless, like the laws of gravity don’t apply. All the controls require additional effort; the 427 is a machine you muscle through the curves. It tolerates the occasional segue through town or a traffic jam, but the 427 makes it clear that its natural state is on open roads, where the Holley carb can inhale plenty of air.


In its day, the 427 was the baddest machine you could buy from a dealer, a crown it wears with pride. It wasn’t until three decades later, when the Dodge Viper hit the streets, that it was equaled.


> The hint of danger is part of the rush. The 427 dares you: *Come on, let’s see what you’ve got.*


## The Ladder


Cameron Neveu


Greene bought his first Cobra, a 1963 260 model with fire damage, for $1000. Imagine that. Of course, that was in 1972, when Cobras were merely used cars. The attraction for the Florida-raised car freak? Big engine, little car.


Back then, Greene worked in construction and earned extra money flipping VW Beetles. In 1979, he and a partner bought a languishing Ford dealership in Blairsville, Georgia, which became the cornerstone of a business that expanded to nine stores, but Greene’s backed off a bit and now has two. As his fortunes rose, Greene bought and sold several Cobras but still owns that original 260. “Look what they did,” he says, about the craftspeople behind the Cobra. “They’re handmade. Every one has a unique character.”


Having kept his cheaply bought first car, Greene’s a bit of an outlier in this group. Most of the members bought Cobras in the ’70s, then sold as prices rose, bought again, and then resisted the urge to take another profit, fearing that climbing values would finally put their dream car out of reach.


The green Cobra was lent by Carroll Shelby to Steve McQueen, who drove it for nine months. It’s now owned by Dave Wagner, a retired Ford engineer.


Cameron Neveu


Kansas City native Jim Sfetko’s Cobra history perfectly illustrates the point. He bought his first Cobra in 1976 for $15,000. A year later, he was offered $34,000 and wasn’t in a position to pass on the tidy 127 percent profit. A decade later, he bought another Cobra, chassis CSX2179, for $38,500. A profitable offer arrived again, but Sfetko declined.


Most of the rally attendees have loved Cobras their whole lives and built careers or businesses that allowed them to buy them when prices were a stretch, but not out of reach. Now they’re all sitting on an heirloom, which presents its own problem.


Not that any of them are complaining. “We’re a lucky group to be here driving Cobras,” someone says at dinner one evening. Nods all around. But they are concerned about what will happen when their cars eventually pass on to the next generation. Seven-figure cars tend to accumulate in vast car collections or museums. Will they be used as Shelby intended?


Cotter’s ’65 Cobra, which he has owned for 26 years, has never been restored. He says it fits like an old pair of jeans.


Cameron Neveu


No one can know. What we do know is that the Cotter-Maxwell rally is an example of what our car hobby can do to create extraordinary experiences and build friendships. Human-centric activities are more important than ever as we’re drawn deeper into the digital world. The U.S. Surgeon General issued a public health advisory in 2023 stating that social isolation is as damaging to our health as smoking 15 cigarettes a day.


“Cars are a catalyst to bring people together,” Cotter says. “We started the rally to enjoy cars, and now 20 years later, we’re most excited just to see each other.” Both Maxwell and Cotter emphasize that, while they love Shelby Cobras, any shared automotive passion can bring people together. It simply requires someone to organize a wet, dirty good time. That someone can be you.


***


## How To Identify a Genuine Shelby Cobra


**1. Body Material:** All original Cobras were aluminum. Some new ones use the material as well, but if the body is thicker fiberglass, it’s a replica.


Cameron Neveu


**2. Serial Numbers:** They’re stamped all over the car, including the frame, the transmission tunnel, the rear bulkhead, and even the door hinges.


Cameron Neveu


**3. Fenders** : Most replicas use the flared fenders of the 427 version. Since only 343 427s were made, if you see a bulging Cobra, it’s likely not real.


Cameron Neveu
